native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 data, socioeconomic status is the primary driver of the racial difference in BA-track educational progress. As of 1979 (ages 14-22), Black students show no overall advantage: 3.6% had completed >=14 grades (2+ years of college) vs 7.4% of non-Black/non-Hispanic students. The Black-non-Black gap is concentrated at low family income (2.7% vs 12.0%; adjusted OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.17-0.53), shrinks at mid income (3.4% vs 4.7%; OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.72-1.98, n.s.) and disappears at high income (6.3% vs 6.7%; OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.57-1.55, n.s.); the Hispanic pattern is identical (Low OR 0.44, Mid 0.94, High 1.21, the latter two n.s.). The race x SES interaction is statistically significant (Black x Mid OR 3.95 [1.86, 8.40]; Black x High OR 3.11 [1.47, 6.60]). Thus, the observed racial gap in BA-track progress is a low-SES phenomenon: at mid and high family income levels, Black and non-Black students reach college progress at statistically indistinguishable rates, so SES level — not race — accounts for the divergence.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection of data/nls_raw.csv (N=12,686 x 61 cols). IMPORTANT: there is NO real BA-completion variable and no post-1979 education waves; the outcome is a proxy — educational progress as of 1979 when respondents were 14-22 years old ('Highest grade completed, 1979' >= 14 = 2+ years of college; code 95 treated as missing). 2) SES constructed (no pre-categorized SES exists): terciles of log1p(total net family income, previous calendar year 1978, recorded 1979) — the most complete pre-outcome measure (80.4% non-missing); income top-coded at 75,001 retained. 3) ASVAB composite (mean of 4 sections) was NOT a real z-score (raw mean ~476, SD ~91) so we standardized it ourselves, z=(x-mean)/sd; because it was measured in 1981 (after the 1979 outcome) it was excluded from primary models and used only as an exploratory sensitivity control. 4) Descriptive cross-tabs of the outcome by race x SES tertile with Wilson 95% CIs. 5) Logistic regressions: M1 race only, M2 +SES, M3 +SES+age+sex+family size (primary), M4 race x SES interaction with cell-specific ORs (vs same-SES non-Black/non-Hispanic reference) with Wald-based 95% CIs. 6) Sensitivity: outcomes >=13 and >=16; SES from 1985 income and 1985 wealth; ASVAB-adjusted model. Analysis sample n=10,071 (listwise: grade + 1979 income available); income missingness is mildly differential by race (Black 17.4% vs Non-Black 20.1%).

sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents aged 14–22 in 1979, with available grade completion and income (n=10,071). sub_hypo.text: SES is hypothesized to be the primary driver of racial differences in BA-track educational progress: the racial gap is a low-SES phenomenon, with statistically indistinguishable Black and non-Black/non-Hispanic progress at middle and high incomes.
